title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI systems created a fabricated news article featuring a fake interview between real public figures about a fake investment platform. The system generated text that mimicked legitimate journalism closely enough to circulate online and deceive readers. This is a model producing false statements presented as factual reporting, deployed in a context where no human editorial review occurred before distribution.

The failure happened at the point where generated content entered public circulation without verification. It would have been caught by basic fact-checking, by confirmation that the interview took place, or by the original figures or news outlets disclaiming the article. The deployment used AI outside the conditions of its intended use, substituting fabrication for journalism.

It is not established whether this particular article was created by a commercial AI system, by a customized tool, or by what process scammers generated it. The broader pattern shows scammers using AI to build entire false ecosystems of articles, reviews, and advertisements around fraudulent schemes, with rising success.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake article recently circulated online featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never occurred. This incident represents a growing type of scam using artificial intelligence to create convincing but false content. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows these deepfake investment schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent.

ASIC's latest data reveals significant rises in online fraud, including a 182 percent increase in total scams removed last year and a 279 percent jump in phishing scams. The regulator also removed over 7,000 fake investment platforms. Scammers commonly impersonate well-known Australians, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart among the most targeted. Rather than using single fake images, sophisticated schemes now create entire fake online ecosystems with fabricated news articles, reviews, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing.
